response:
READING

**The numbers first**

Current book: £2.1m on 148t. Four jigs at 41t each = 164t ceiling; current utilisation 90%.

MORVEDD revenue: Thurlmere 96t × £15.40 = £1,478,400 plus Marchgate 65t × £14.19 = £922,350, total roughly £2,401k. Against the current £2.1m that is a gross gain of about £300k a year, or £900k across the term before the £96k capex. The net three-year advantage over SALTGRAVE is therefore somewhere around £810k. That is a real and substantial number and it must be treated seriously.

SALTGRAVE revenue: Marchgate £922k plus Thurlmere at current level £653k plus Ostrey 37t × £14.60 = £540k, total roughly £2,115k — marginally ahead of today even without the Thurlmere expansion, because Ostrey's rate rises and Ostrey moves from an informal arrangement onto a three-year commitment. Zero capital out.

**The Marchgate background risk**

Marchgate is 44% of turnover and has signed nothing. That risk exists identically in both courses and should be set to one side for the purpose of comparing them; it neither favours nor disfavours MORVEDD relative to SALTGRAVE. The correct action — whether or not the Thurlmere decision is taken — is to pursue a Marchgate contract, but that is a separate matter.

**The Vennerdale/change-of-control problem: why it is disqualifying rather than merely adverse**

Thurlmere was acquired by the Vennerdale group only in 2025, twelve months ago at most. Vennerdale is plainly active in the sector; that acquisition happened and now they are aggressively expanding Thurlmere's commission-dyeing volume. Active acquirers resell, merge and restructure. The base rate of a further change-of-control event at a recently-purchased business over a subsequent three-year window is meaningfully elevated — considerably higher than for a long-established independent.

The draft contract allows either party to exit on six months' notice on a change of control. From Gallowfield's standpoint this clause offers no real protection. Six months' notice on a customer that, under MORVEDD, would be 62% of turnover (£1.478m of £2.401m) means the following scenario has to be lived with for the entire three-year term:

> At any point Vennerdale completes a further transaction, the notice clock starts, and Gallowfield has six months to replace £1.478m of revenue from a standing start with 19 staff, two jigs half-committed to infrastructure built for Thurlmere's cloth, Ostrey gone to another dyer (22-year relationships do not come back), £96,000 already spent, and a cash reserve of £180,000.

That is not a recoverable position in six months. Total revenue would fall from £2.4m to roughly £922k — Marchgate only, still contract-free — before any replacement work could be won. Nineteen staff cannot be supported on £922k, and winning commission-dyeing work quickly enough to bridge the gap is implausible when the trade knows you are in distress.

The probability that this change-of-control scenario materialises is genuinely uncertain, but it does not need to be high to be disqualifying: because the consequence if it does materialise is insolvency or near-insolvency, not a bad year.

**The Ostrey dimension**

Ostrey's offer — 37t for three years at £14.60/kg — is a known, bounded, immediately securable benefit. It locks in 25% of the book at a rate better than the current average, from a customer with a 22-year loyalty record. Its offer expires 28 November 2026, so even if the Thurlmere decision is taken by 31 October, there is time to accept Ostrey's terms. Releasing Ostrey to accommodate MORVEDD means ending a relationship that Ostrey cannot reverse; they will find alternative capacity. Burning a 22-year counterparty for a three-year contract with a recently-acquired company is a poor exchange on straightforward probability grounds, before any measure of reputation effects in the trade.

**The capital and flexibility point**

£96,000 is more than half the liquid reserve. Spending it produces infrastructure that is useful only if Thurlmere delivers the full three years. The dedicated pumps and liquor circuit have limited application if Thurlmere exits; the jigs themselves are reusable, but the associated investment is not. Under SALTGRAVE, the £96,000 stays in the business, the bank facility remains untouched, and all four jigs remain available for any combination of customers. Flexibility has genuine value in a business with a 164t hard ceiling and uncertain demand.

**The comparison restated**

MORVEDD offers roughly £810k of net incremental value over three years against SALTGRAVE, but it delivers that value only if the Thurlmere contract runs its full course without a Vennerdale change of control. If the change-of-control clause is exercised — even once, at any point in the three years — the value reverses sharply and the business faces a crisis it probably cannot navigate. The expected value of MORVEDD is therefore heavily weighted by the probability and timing of a Vennerdale event, which is elevated precisely because Vennerdale bought Thurlmere only last year. A business of this scale (£2.1m, 19 staff, £180k liquid) should not carry existential tail risk for an expected value improvement of this magnitude when a viable, lower-risk alternative is on the table.

SALTGRAVE foregoes the premium but: keeps three counterparties, largest at 44%; locks Ostrey in for three years at an improved rate; puts no capital at risk; preserves full jig flexibility; and avoids structural dependence on a company that has already changed hands once and whose new owner has a near-term incentive to keep moving.

The one genuine weakness in SALTGRAVE is that declining Thurlmere's offer may lead them to find a committed dyer and take their 46t current business elsewhere, reducing SALTGRAVE revenue from roughly £2.1m to roughly £1.46m. That is painful, not existential. The business can run at £1.46m while seeking replacement tonnage, it cannot survive losing 62% at six months' notice with the book already shrunken.

**Verdict**

SALTGRAVE is the sounder course. The Thurlmere premium is real but priced too cheaply for the risk it carries.

---

READING
Gallowfield's cash reserve is £180k, Thurlmere would be 62% of a £2.4m book under MORVEDD, the draft contract carries a six-month exit on change of control, and Vennerdale acquired Thurlmere only twelve months ago — meaning a further change-of-control event during the contract term is a plausible rather than remote contingency. If that clause fires, revenue falls from £2.4m to roughly £922k with six months' warning, Ostrey has already been released to a competitor, and £96k of dedicated infrastructure sits stranded. No firm of this scale and liquidity can absorb that cleanly. SALTGRAVE locks Ostrey in for three years at an improved rate, keeps a three-name book with the largest customer at 44%, preserves the full capital reserve and jig flexibility, and avoids existential dependence on a recently-acquired counterparty. The revenue foregone (~£302k/year) is the real cost and it is not trivial; but it is a cost, not a catastrophe, whereas the downside of MORVEDD if Vennerdale moves again is a catastrophe.

CALL
SALTGRAVE

GROUNDS
Concentrating 62% of revenue in a customer whose 2025 acquirer retains a six-month change-of-control exit right creates a plausible single-event path to insolvency that cannot be justified by the £302,000-a-year premium for a business with £180,000 in liquid reserves.
